title: Venerable Master Xuyun at Yunju Mountain
author: Master Shaoyun
excerpt: Venerable elders, honored Dharma masters, lay practitioners, and faithful friends:

inline.s: Venerable elders, honored Dharma masters, lay practitioners, and faithful friends:

I would like to take this occasion to give the Buddhists of Hong Kong a brief account of the Venerable Master Xuyun's deeds and way of life at Yunju Mountain, hoping that his many fine words and exemplary conduct may serve as a model for those of us in later generations who study the Dharma. At the same time, I wish to offer this modest token in commemoration of the fortieth anniversary of the Elder's passing, as a small repayment of his kindness in nourishing me with the Dharma. As my own cultivation is shallow and my understanding of the Dharma limited, if there are any errors or shortcomings, I beg the compassionate guidance of all the great worthies.

In August 1956 I left Hanshan County in Anhui Province and came to Zhenru Monastery on Yunju Mountain in Yongxiu County, Jiangxi, to seek refuge with the Venerable Master Xuyun and to request ordination. I was nineteen that year, and after graduating from high school I left home for Yunju Mountain. In fact, ever since I was sixteen I had been writing in secret to the Elder behind my family's back, and though he was a great and eminent master known throughout China and abroad, he always answered my letters personally. When I met the Elder he asked me why I wished to leave home. I said it was to become a Buddha. Delighted at this, he took me as a disciple and shaved my head himself, giving me the name Xuande and the style Shaoyun. That winter I went to Nanhua Monastery to receive the complete precepts. I then returned to Yunju Monastery to dwell and to join the assembly in daily labor. A few months later I began to attend upon the Elder, and by day I listened to the Abbot, Master Haideng, expound the scriptures at the monastery.

That year the Elder was one hundred and seventeen years old, more than two meters tall, with hands that hung past his knees and eyes that shone with piercing brightness; at night he read the small print of newspapers by lamplight without ever wearing glasses. He had thirty-six teeth, all neat and intact, and he said they had grown anew only after he passed ninety. His voice was extraordinarily sonorous; sometimes when he lectured in the meditation hall, the sudden volume of it set the hall's timekeeping bell humming. When the Elder came to Yunju Mountain in July 1953, the mountain was covered in rubble and wild grass, with only three dilapidated buildings and four monks remaining — the bleak scene left after the halls and towers of Zhenru Monastery had been destroyed by the artillery fire of Japanese soldiers on March 19, 1939.

Within a few months of the Elder's arrival at Yunju Mountain, more than fifty people had come, and once they had met him none were willing to leave. He therefore petitioned the government to rebuild Yunju Mountain and, once it was approved, set to work without delay. To make the community self-sufficient he began to open up wasteland and plant crops. By the time I arrived in 1956, nearly a hundred mu of paddy fields and more than sixty mu of dry fields had been reclaimed, yielding sixty to seventy thousand jin of rice and seventy to eighty thousand jin of sweet potatoes and potatoes each year.

Afterward the people grew more and more numerous, and the monastery then ruled that those without labor power or the ability to produce would not be permitted to take lodging. By the end of 1956 there were more than one hundred and twenty residents, with over two hundred mu of reclaimed land and over a hundred mu of dry fields; each year nearly a hundred thousand jin of rice and more than a hundred thousand jin of miscellaneous grains were harvested, so that the community was essentially self-sufficient.

Then already one hundred and seventeen years old, the Elder went every day to the construction sites and the lands being opened up, directing the work himself, and he received visitors from every quarter. At six in the evening he lectured in the meditation hall, and after eight o'clock he began to go through letters from all over the country; sometimes more than a hundred arrived in a single day, and he read every one. If a letter was important he replied in his own hand; for ordinary letters he would state the gist and we answered on his behalf. He usually did not rest until about midnight, then rose at two in the morning to sit in meditation, and only when the fourth board sounded — about three-thirty — did he get up to wash his face.

He used no toothbrush or toothpaste; he merely rinsed his mouth with warm water, spat it onto a towel, and first washed his eyes, then washed his whole face. He said that washing this way guarded against eye disease and strengthened one's sight. After washing his face he would bow before the Buddha, then return to the bed to sit in meditation. At that time we would begin the morning service. After the morning service and a brief rest, at the sound of the wooden clapper the assembly would go to the dining hall for the morning meal.

Life on the mountain was then very hard: little land had been cultivated and the grain harvested was scant. Because sweet potatoes were hardy and yielded well, from July of each year until the following March was the season for eating them. The leaves and stems of the sweet potatoes were our vegetables; sometimes there were not even roots and leaves to be had, only fried salt to mix into the congee. The congee we ate each morning was made from only a little rice boiled with a great many sweet potatoes. As for the midday meal, though the masters ate a great deal, they had only a little plain vegetable; a dish of greens was already a luxury. In the evening there was no rice or noodles, only boiled sweet potatoes or potatoes set out in the dining hall, and those who wished to take a late meal could help themselves — but very few did.

The congee and vegetables the Elder ate were fetched by us from the great kitchen and were the same as those the masters of the assembly ate. Unless there were guests, he never added a single extra dish. Even now, when we think of that frugal and simple life of his, it remains fresh in our memory.

Yunju Mountain stands very high, at more than eleven hundred meters above sea level. The winters there were bitterly cold, falling to seventeen or eighteen degrees below zero. The sweet potatoes stored in the cellar could not withstand the cold air; their skins turned black, and once boiled they tasted bitter.

One time when Master Qixian and I were eating congee at the Elder's place, we tasted the bitter and astringent sweet-potato skins, picked them out, and set them on the edge of the table. The Elder saw this but said nothing; after we had finished eating, he quietly picked up those skins and ate them all. Witnessing this, the two of us felt deeply ashamed and grieved. From then on we did not dare refuse the skins of the sweet potatoes.

Afterward we asked him, 'You are of such an advanced age, Master, and those skins were so bitter — how could you eat them?' The Elder sighed and said to us, 'This is food! It is only to be eaten, never to be wasted.'

On another occasion, Mr. Zhang Jianming, head of the Religious Affairs Office of Jiangxi Province, came up the mountain to visit the Elder. The Elder added several dishes himself and invited him to lunch. Director Zhang was after all a layman who did not understand the cherishing of blessings. While eating he dropped several grains of rice on the ground. The Elder saw it but said nothing, and only after the meal did he bend down himself, pick up each grain of rice from the floor one by one, and put it into his mouth. This left Director Zhang red-faced and ill at ease. He urged the Elder again and again, 'Venerable Master, those grains fell on the floor and are dirty; you cannot eat them.' The Elder said, 'It is nothing! All of this is food; not a single grain may be wasted.' The director added, 'You really should improve your living conditions, Master!' The Elder answered, 'As it is, I am already very well off.'

The Elder was in good health. In the morning, besides two bowls of congee, he would sometimes eat a little potato. At noon he ate two large bowls of rice. In the evening he sometimes took a small bowl of noodles or a little congee. He said that he had begun to take the evening meal only after the Yunmen incident; until then he had always observed the rule of not eating after noon.

His teeth were especially good. I remember once a lay devotee sent some roasted fava beans up the mountain. Seeing us eating them, the Elder wanted some too. We said, 'These are very hard, Master — can your teeth manage them?' Without a word he picked up the beans and began to eat, and he ate faster than we did. We were quite surprised.

He was most frugal and careful to cherish his blessings. When the straw mat he slept on tore, he had us mend it with cloth. Before long it tore again in the same place, indeed beyond mending. We said we would take the mat to the monastery and exchange it for a new one. At that time a straw mat cost only about two yuan; yet when the Elder heard this he scolded us loudly, 'What great fortune! To enjoy a new mat at the monastery's expense!' None of us dared utter a word.

Whether in winter or summer, the Elder wore only a worn-out patched robe — a long garment mended again and again (which the Chan practitioners call the hundred-patch robe). In winter he added a padded coat beneath it, and in summer wore only a single thin undergarment.

The Elder often taught us, 'To cultivate wisdom one must understand the principle; to cultivate blessings there is nothing better than to cherish them.' He meant that one who cultivates wisdom and practices Chan must understand the principle, and the principle is the road ahead. If you wish to practice Chan with effort but cannot discern the road ahead and have not grasped the principle of Chan, you will find it very difficult to make progress in your work. Hence the ancients said, 'In cultivation there is nothing else to cultivate; the key is to know the road ahead. Once you know the road ahead, birth and death together come to rest.' As for cherishing blessings, how could a monk, by rights, have money with which to build merit? In truth, 'to create blessings there is nothing better than to cherish them' — that is, to value every blessed condition in one's own life. He would frequently admonish us of the younger generation, saying, 'You must cherish your blessings! That you can now encounter the Dharma and come here to cultivate with me may be owing to a little merit you planted in past lives. But if you do not cherish your blessings and squander them all, you will become a person without merit. It is like having made money in business in the past and deposited it in the bank. If you now no longer work diligently to earn, but only give yourself to enjoyment until you have spent every one of your savings, then before long you will fall into debt.'

And so the Elder's demands of us were very strict. I feel that we monastics today enjoy far too great a store of blessings; in clothing, food, shelter, and travel, our lives are many times more plentiful than in the past. Therefore, within such blessings, we should all the more take care to cherish them. A person endowed with merit and virtue will cultivate more smoothly; one without merit and virtue, whatever method he practices, will meet with all manner of hindrances.

The Elder once told us that he shaved his head only once a year, on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, and washed his feet only on the evening of that same day. That is why in photographs his hair and beard appear so long. But after 1952 he would shave his head and wash his feet once every two months, or sometimes once a month. His eyebrows were extraordinary: from the end of each brow there grew several long hairs, which within less than half a month reached six or seven inches and hung down to his jaw. Sometimes, finding them in the way when he washed his face or ate, he would pluck them out with one hand, but before long they grew again. At the time we kept his hair and those long eyebrow hairs; only during the Cultural Revolution were they taken away.

He also said that he never bathed in his whole life. Then, in the great heat, what did he do when he sweated? In hot weather he would sometimes perspire, but each time he had to be urged again and again by us, and only after several days would he reluctantly change his clothing once. Strange to say, the clothes he took off had not the least smell of sweat. The cloth socks he wore especially he often changed only once every half month or month, and they too had no odor. The Elder's practice and conduct were indeed unlike those of ordinary people.

Although the Elder was already over one hundred and ten years old, his strength was beyond all measure. A master who had once lived with the Elder at Yunmen Monastery said that once, when they were opening wasteland at Yunmen, there was a great boulder that several people together could not move; when the Elder came, he told them all to stand aside and, alone, carried that great boulder far away.

One day in the latter half of 1957, I had just come back from outside when I saw the Elder walking toward the great kitchen carrying two large bundles of firewood in both hands, and I asked, 'Master, why have you come here to carry firewood?' At my question he set the wood down and returned to his quarters. I went to the kitchen to find Master Zixing, who was in charge of chopping firewood, and told him what I had seen. He said in astonishment, 'I chopped three large bundles of wood and carried one back to the kitchen myself. I left the other two by the path west of the thatched hut; they were so heavy that I could not lift even one. How can the Elder have such strength as to pick up both bundles at once!' Later I helped him weigh one of those bundles, and a single one weighed over two hundred jin. So the Elder's strength truly could not be measured. For one who cultivates, the harsher the circumstances, the firmer the resolve on the Way. The Elder often said, 'Without enduring the bitter cold that pierces the bones, how could the plum blossom send forth its fragrance?'

Life at Yunju Mountain was then extremely hard, with a great deal of laborious and intense work. Besides farming, building the temple, and raising houses, as well as the daily sitting and the service in the hall, the masters had to mark out and reclaim a very large area of wasteland each day; if it could not be finished by daylight, they would keep working after dark until the goal was met.

Sometimes goods had to be carried up the mountain. On moonlit nights, after the rest incense and the four incense periods, they would still have to go thirty li down the mountain and carry loads back up. Having rested less than two hours upon return, they would have to attend the morning service. After the morning service and the morning meal they sat the early board incense for only half an hour before the board sounded and they went out to labor. Life was therefore very intense and busy, yet the masters' resolve on the Way was steadfast.

Moreover, at night they had to stand watch in pairs, each pair for two hours at a time in turn, to guard the paddy fields against wild boars, for at that time the mountain had many boars and tigers. Once the grain flowered and was nearly ripe, the boars came in droves. As soon as a single boar cried out, dozens of others would come at the sound and fall upon the stalks of grain in the fields, so that a large stretch of paddies could vanish in a single stroke.

Though the Elder was of such advanced years, he insisted on joining our night watch over the paddy fields. At that time Master Haideng was abbot on the mountain, and seeing the Elder labor thus, he too came to take part in the assembly's rotating night watch against the wild boars.

On Yunju Mountain the Elder not only frequently ascended the hall to give the assembly of masters instruction, but also set a personal example through his actions in the countless details of daily life, teaching the assembly thereby. Now when we look back, we feel utterly ashamed. Truly, every movement and every word of a good spiritual friend is a model for those of us who come after.

In the Yunmen incident the Elder's bones were broken in several places. Between 1956 and 1958 he was often ill and feverish; when the old injuries and the places where bones had been broken ached beyond bearing, he would lie on his bed moaning. Yet the moment he heard that someone had come to see him, he would at once sit up, crossing his legs, in excellent spirits, and could converse for three or four hours without the least sign of illness. Sometimes we urged the guests to leave so that he might rest, but he was displeased and scolded us, saying, 'People come to me only when they have business to settle; we must let them leave only after they have said everything.' But the moment the guests were gone he would lie back down and moan. We asked him, 'Just now, when people came, you were in such good spirits; the moment they left, why are you in such pain again?' He said, 'This is the power of karma! Even King Yama cannot govern me. When I want to rise, I rise; when I do not want to rise, I do not.' In truth we found it most wondrous.

In the first month of 1957 the Elder fell gravely ill, and cadres from Yongxiu County and the provincial government came to visit him and sent a car to take him to the provincial hospital in Nanchang. He had not wanted to go, but the provincial leaders urged and pressed him again and again until he reluctantly agreed. Once in the hospital, when they examined him and tested his blood type, the medical staff were astonished. They said, 'We hear this venerable elder is over a hundred years old, yet his blood type is like that of a child under thirteen; we have never seen such a blood type in a person of so great an age.' After careful testing they said the Elder's blood type was purely yang. Yet the Elder stayed in the hospital only four days before returning to the mountain. His blood type remains a mystery to this day.

When he rested at noon he would sometimes grow drowsy, his head drooping forward and even snoring. Once, hearing him snore, we slipped away in secret and took the fruit from the room outside, eating and playing as we went. When he woke he scolded us for each thing we had done. We asked, 'Master, were you not just now asleep and snoring? How could you know?' He said, 'I know even how many deluded thoughts pass through your mind — do you think I would not know that you took things outside to eat?' From then on we believed that one who has awakened to the Way and transcended birth and death has already broken through the five aggregates. He appeared to be asleep, yet his mind was perfectly clear and lucid.
Taking the opportunity, we also asked the Elder about his life in a thatched hut on Zhongnan Mountain.

That year he was sixty-seven, dwelling in a thatched hut on Zhongnan Mountain. Master Jiechen, a teacher of the greater sutras, having heard that the Elder had awakened at Gaomin Monastery, came to the hut on Zhongnan Mountain to debate with him the sharp, cryptic sayings of the Chan school. The Elder, hearing him speak with such grand claims, said to him, 'Your word-play in debate is very fine, but this is not your own true practice; when it comes to the very root of birth and death, you are not in control, and King Yama will not let you off. Let us debate no more — you and I will sit together for a while.' So the two of them sat in meditation in the hut. The Elder sat for seven days and seven nights, unmoving and serene. Master Jiechen, however, could sit only half a day before both his legs ached beyond bearing and the delusions in his mind grew ever more restless and agitated.

Every day Master Jiechen walked several circles around the Elder, and it was with great difficulty that he waited until the seventh day, when the Elder at last emerged from samādhi. He asked the Elder, 'While you were in concentration, were you aware, or were you not aware? If you were aware, it could not be called entering concentration; if you were not aware, would that not be a withered concentration — what is called a dead pool that cannot harbor a dragon?' The Elder said, 'You must know that this method of the Chan school does not take concentration as its final goal; it seeks only to clear the mind and see the nature. When true doubt is present, the mind is naturally pure. Because the sense of doubt is unbroken, it is not a state of unknowing; and because there is no deluded thought, it is not a state of knowing. Though there is no knowing through deluded thought, even a needle dropped on the ground can be heard distinctly; and I knew when you walked your circles around me each day, only that through the power of doubt no discrimination arose. Though no discrimination arose, because the doubt was present and its function unceasing, it was not a withered concentration. Yet though it was not a withered concentration, this is still only a matter along the path of practice, not itself the final goal. Thus these past seven days have seemed to me as though they passed in the snap of a finger; had I given rise to even one discriminating thought, I would have emerged from concentration. One who practices Chan and works on the Way must press this doubt to the very utmost; and when the moment and the conditions arrive, and he breaks through the mass of doubt and touches his own nose, that is true accord with the unborn.' From then on Master Jiechen followed the Elder always, with deep conviction and reverence.

Later there was a time when the Elder entered samādhi for eighteen days; when the others on the mountain learned of it, they all came to pay their respects to him. Finding this wearisome, the two of them shouldered their packs and set out for Mount Emei. One night they lodged in a small, deserted, rundown temple. The Elder said that in the middle of the night a flea bit Master Jiechen, and he set the flea down on the ground; the flea toppled over and broke its leg, and the Elder, in his concentration, heard the flea cry out most pitiably. The next day the Elder asked Master Jiechen about this. In amazement he thought, 'He even knew that I set a flea on the ground, and heard its cries as well — how extraordinary is the power of his concentration!' From this one may know how inconceivable is the state of body and mind at perfect peace.

Later the two of them went together to Yunnan to establish a place of practice. At that time, in 1957, several old masters at Yunju Mountain, over eighty years old, knew of these matters. They said that the venerable Master Jiechen too was remarkable, and that in the end, knowing in advance the time of his passing, he first took leave of the assembly and then passed away in a seated position.

During his time in Yunnan, the Elder would often sit for seven or eight days at a stretch. Sometimes, when people had urgent matters to discuss with him, they had to strike the small gong to rouse him from concentration before he would emerge. Thus, when the Elder was at Yunju Mountain, we asked him, 'Were these things really so?' He said, 'Yes.' We asked again, 'Then why, Master, do you not enter concentration now?' He said, 'Now that the monastery is being rebuilt, government officials and others come to see me every day, and if I do not come out it will not do — so I cannot enter concentration.' Then he added with a smile, 'If I were to sit here for seven or eight days without rising, some ill-intentioned persons, thinking me dead, would carry off this body of mine and burn it. Then the monastery could not be built. So now I dare not enter concentration.'

Although during his time at Yunju Mountain the Elder never sat in concentration for as long as seven or eight days, he would often sit for an entire day without moving. Sometimes he began to sit at about midnight and did not rise until the following evening. So the stage he had attained is not something an ordinary person could know.

We once asked the Elder, 'We have heard that one who has realized the Way is a sage, is that so?' He said, 'Yes.' I said, 'Then that is one who has realized the first fruit, the arhat — is that not so?' 'The first fruit — yes,' he said. He continued, 'In fact the first fruit is no small thing. One who has realized the first fruit, the srotaāpanna, has no deluded thoughts not only in concentration but in his ordinary daily life of going, staying, sitting, and lying down. His six faculties do not become defiled by the six objects; that is, the six objects cannot disturb him. He has entered the stream of the noble ones.'

It is said that when one who has realized the first fruit walks, though you may see both his feet set upon the ground, in truth they are two fen above it. At that time people also asked us, 'We have heard that one who has transcended birth and death walks without his feet touching the ground or his shoes taking up mud. Since the Elder is a great bodhisattva, and you often walk with him, tell us plainly — do his feet touch the ground or not? Do his shoes take up mud or not?' So we paid close attention to this matter and tested it many times.

The ground at Yunju Mountain was all clay, and it rained often. When an ordinary person walked a stretch and came back, his shoes would naturally be covered with mud; yet the Elder's shoes never showed any mud. Strangely, when we walked behind him and watched attentively how he went, we plainly saw his shoes pressing into the muddy earth; but upon returning and looking at his shoes, they bore not the slightest trace of mud. The mystery of this we have never been able to fathom.

In 1957 a fire broke out on the mountain outside the pass at Zhenru Monastery, and the masters of the assembly all went to fight it. The Elder told us to follow him too. At first he wore a short inner robe and walked briskly ahead; but when he reached the area outside Zhao Zhou Pass and was about to go up the mountain, the Elder ahead of us suddenly vanished, and there he was standing on a great rock several zhang away from us. We could not help shouting, 'Master, you were just here a moment ago — how did you get so far away all at once!' Standing on the height, he called, 'Hurry and fight the fire!' We truly could not tell how he had crossed the distance.

At that time the Elder lectured in the meditation hall every evening, or sometimes every other day. As soon as the time came and the summoning board was struck with a crack, not only did the masters — those of us in the fields and those out at labor — come running back, but even the crows in the sky would flock down to hear the lecture. At that time the crows at Yunju Mountain were especially numerous; the rooftops, the nearby trees, and the path from the thatched hut to the meditation hall were all crowded dense with them, so that we could hardly take a step. Sometimes we had to stir them with a staff; only when they hopped aside was there room to pass, or we would have stepped on them. When the lecture ended and the Elder returned to his hut, the crows too returned to their nests. So it may be said that even birds are possessed of a fine spiritual awareness.

In the first ten days of June 1957 the weather was scorching hot. One day the Elder suddenly wished to go up to the summit of the Five Old Men Peak to survey the terrain. Six of us went — Qingkong, Jingxing, Master Chuanyin, myself, and others. We lashed two bamboo poles to a rattan armchair to make a small sedan chair for the Elder to ride in, and we relieved one another in three shifts. When we set out it was nearly nine o'clock, the weather very hot and the sun fierce. We thought to ourselves, 'The Elder is of such weak constitution, and the weather so hot, that he should choose today of all days to go to the summit of the Five Old Men Peak; he is sure to suffer terribly in the sun.' Strange to say, the moment we lifted the sedan chair, a great many crows came flying from the sky, gathered and circled above the chair, and shaded the sun so completely that we were not in the least exposed to its rays. They followed us all the way; wherever the chair was carried, the crows circled above like a dark cloud, so that we felt no heat at all.

We went on until the summit of the Five Old Men Peak, and when the Elder stepped down from the chair, the crows at once flew down, clustered about the chair, and, raising their heads, cawed at the Elder without cease. The Elder lingered on the summit a while, surveyed the terrain on all sides, and then turned back. As soon as we lifted the chair, the crows again swarmed up into the sky and, as on the way out, circled above us, forming a great canopy that blocked the fierce sunlight until we reached the door of the thatched hut, when they gradually dispersed.

Once inside the hut, the Elder said, 'You were all afraid that today would be unbearably hot — well, was it hot?' The six of us could only smile a taut smile. We said, 'Today it was wholly due to your blessing and virtue, Master, that moved those crows to come and protect the Dharma by shading the sun. But for that, with such fierce sunlight, our going and returning would have been most unpleasant!' So when a man of the Way stirs a single thought, even the flock of birds comes to his protection.

In July 1955 the Elder's thatched hut was burned down, and the outer wall of the adjoining little kitchen also collapsed. It was an earthen wall, built by setting two boards together and ramming earth in between. The masters building the wall then were Jingxing, Qingkong, and two others, four in all. They had only just poured in the earth when, it being afternoon, black clouds rolled up in the western sky, threatening a heavy storm. The four wall-builders grew anxious, for a newly built earthen wall is not firm and would collapse if soaked by rain. Among them Master Jingxing said, 'The Elder is sitting at the door; let us go and ask him to stir a thought and will this rain not to come here.' The other three agreed. So Jingxing went and bowed to the Elder, saying, 'Master, in your compassion, our earthen wall has only just been finished; if it rains it will collapse. It must not rain.' The Elder looked at the sky, said not a word, and rose to go back to his quarters.

After a while a great wind arose and the heavy rain followed, wind and rain together; but when the rain reached the house west of the hut, less than five feet from the earthen wall, it simply ceased. It went on raining for over an hour, the water pouring endlessly from the roofs, yet around the hut with its newly built earthen wall there was not a single drop. When the wind and rain had passed, the four of them ran overjoyed to bow to the Elder and thank him for his help. The Elder gave no sound and said nothing.

The ancients said, 'Where the Way is lofty, even dragons and tigers bow; where virtue is weighty, even ghosts and spirits honor.' This is true beyond doubt. When the Elder stirred a single thought, it was as though even the dragon king of the sea had to obey, and where he would not have the rain fall, the rain did not reach.

In the middle of May 1957, the rice seedlings had only recently been transplanted in the fields. The mountain had seen several days of heavy rain, and a flash flood broke out, sweeping away even the Anle Bridge. The floodwaters, bearing small stones and sand, overran the banks of the mountain stream and were about to rush into the paddies. It was about noon. Master Hongqing had just come out of the little kitchen when he was astonished to find the Elder alone in the wind and rain, without an umbrella, clad in his patched robe and wearing arhat straw sandals, walking slowly eastward along the Anle Bridge embankment toward the rice fields. He at once hurried to fetch an umbrella, and, holding open his own, ran to the Elder.

Strangely, he found that wherever the Elder had passed, the floodwaters did not rush into the paddies but instead flowed eastward along the mountain, rising several feet above the edge of the fields and the stream banks — that is, the flood did not flow down to the low places but surged up to the heights! And in this way the freshly transplanted paddies were spared the disaster of being buried beneath the flood's water and sand.

Afterward the Elder walked to the Buddha-Seal Bridge and stood there. Master Hongqing returned to summon the prior, Master Yinkai, and when the prior learned of it, he arranged for the work board to be struck and himself went to the Elder, asking, 'In such heavy rain, Master, how is it that you have come out alone?' The Elder said, 'If I had not come out, the several tens of mu of paddy fields above would have been lost, all buried beneath the mud and sand of the flood — and then where would there be any grain to harvest?'

We saw then that the Elder's patched robe bore but few raindrops, and only the arhat straw sandals he wore had been soaked by the rain. Truly, where a man of the Way passes, even the waters yield the way.

The Elder's dignified deportment in going, staying, sitting, and lying down was most correct, and he truly fulfilled the saying, 'Walk like the wind, stand like a pine, sit like a bell, lie like a bow.' When he stood, his hands hung at his sides, his neck against his collar, and he walked straight and upright. He often told us, 'When the body is straight, the shadow is not skewed' — that is, if the body is upright, the shadow is surely straight. He meant thereby that one who works at the Way, if he holds a straightforward heart, is certain to succeed.
Every word the Elder spoke throughout his life was a guide to us; every movement he made was an example for those who came after.

In his lifetime the Elder built more than eighty small temples and revived six great monasteries, including Zhusheng Monastery on Jizu Mountain in Yunnan, Yunqi Monastery in Kunming, Nanhua Monastery in Qujiang, Guangdong, Yunmen Monastery in Ruyuan, Yongquan Monastery on Gushan in Fujian, and Zhenru Monastery on Yunju Mountain in Jiangxi. So that the five lineages of the Chan school might be handed down without interruption, he personally inherited and passed them on, becoming the forty-third patriarch of the Linji lineage, the forty-seventh of the Caodong lineage, the eighth of the Weiyang lineage, the eighth of the Fayan lineage, and the twelfth of the Yunmen lineage. He personally tonsured more than a thousand monastic disciples, and his lay disciples, at home and abroad, numbered over a million. For this reason he is called the foremost authority of the Chan school in our age.

In 1958, during the period of socialist education, some people of ultra-leftist tendencies, making use of certain unprincipled monks, slandered the Elder. Because he was a member of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, he could not be branded a counter-revolutionary; they could only strike at his reputation. So they put up many wall posters full of falsehoods about him. The Elder read them without saying a word and, at the meeting, expressed his thanks. Yet the anguish in his heart was beyond words.

After 1958 he told us, 'I am going to leave.' Grieved, we asked, 'How is it that you must go now?' He replied, 'You do not know. There are yet ten more years of suffering to come — how hard it will be!' At the time we did not understand; later there came the ten years of havoc of the Cultural Revolution.
From 1958 onward the Elder was often troubled by minor illnesses, so he gradually handed over each affair to his successors and distributed all his possessions to the assembly.

At three o'clock in the afternoon of September 10, 1959, the Elder gave his final instruction and testament to the assembly, saying, 'My last words are only these: diligently cultivate precepts, meditation, and wisdom, and extinguish greed, hatred, and delusion.' A moment later he added, 'With right mindfulness and a right mind, nurture a fearless spirit, to deliver people and the world.' The Elder admonished us to observe the precepts and practice well.

At noon on September 12, 1959, the Elder said to his attendant, 'Just now in my dream I saw an ox trample and break the stone slabs of the Buddha-Seal Bridge, and I saw the waters of the Emerald Stream cut off.' Then he closed his eyes and was silent. Until half past twelve he called the attendants in and said to them, 'You have served me for many years and have all labored hard. I will say little of the past. For nearly ten years I have endured every hardship, day after day amid danger and doubt, suffering slander and flattery, and I have willingly borne it all, wishing only to preserve for our land the monasteries of the Buddhas and patriarchs, to keep for the temple the pure standards of the virtuous founders, and to preserve for the monks this single robe (kāṣāya). This robe I fought with all my might to win back; you are all my disciples of the inner room and know the course of it. Henceforth, whether you build a thatched hut with a roof of rushes over your heads, or go forth to teach in all directions, you must firmly keep this one robe. But how can it be preserved forever? There is but one word, and that is: 'precepts.' Upon finishing, the Elder joined his palms and said farewell to all; the assembly withdrew in tears and waited beneath the eaves outside.'

At a quarter to two in the afternoon, in his thatched hut on Yunju Mountain, the Elder lay on his right side in the auspicious lion posture and passed away in peace. In the month before his passing, many masters had seen a great light issue from the hut and move toward the Grand Hall; they saw only a bright halo, with no form within, and only as it entered the hall did it gradually fade. More than a month later, after setting all affairs in order and writing out his testament in his own hand, the Elder bade the two attendants retire and, alone in the hut, quietly departed.

The Elder passed away on the twelfth of September, was placed in the coffin on the nineteenth, and was cremated the following day. It was expected that three days later the furnace would be opened to gather the relics and ashes. But unexpectedly, the next day a fire broke out on the mountain outside the Zhao Zhou Pass, where nearly a hundred people lived; the whole assembly went to fight the fire, leaving only the old, the weak, and the sick in the temple. Among them, Master Kuanhuai and Master Kuanke ran outside the cremation furnace and peered in, and saw the Elder's ashes sitting upright and unmoved, just as a person sits cross-legged. Astonished, they picked up a shard of tile and threw it at the ashes, whereupon the whole heap collapsed. Kuanhuai thrust in his hand and grasped a handful of ashes and, seeing several bright, lustrous relics, immediately cried out.

A moment later, those who had fought the fire returned one after another, and hearing that the Elder's ashes held relics, they rushed over, each grabbing a handful of ashes and running off into the quiet places of the mountain, for at that time the government's circumstances would not allow the word 'relics' to be spoken. Dozens did this; in some handfuls there were several relics, in the least one or two, of sizes great and small and colors various, most of them white and translucent. So how many relics were in the Elder's ashes simply can never be counted.

When the dozens of men returned from the fire and were all scrambling thus, Abbot Xingfu had no choice but to call Master Huitong, Master Zixiu, and several others to sift the ashes, and many more relics were sifted out. Among them Master Huitong picked up one relic larger than a thumb, crystal-pure and translucent, which he later gave to Master Haideng, who had come from afar upon hearing the news. It is said that Master Haideng took the relic to Mount Tiantai in Zhejiang. At that time a certain Master Dading, who had been planting vegetables in the garden, only learned the news later; when he arrived, he could only pick up a piece of bone. He carried the bone back to the garden and broke it, discovering within a blood-red relic the size of a red bean, together with a smaller one clinging to the bone.

There was also a Master Yiru, last to return from fighting the fire, who upon hearing of the relics dashed with flying steps to the cremation furnace. But by then there was nothing left but a stretch of bare ground, even the ashes swept clean. He could not help crying aloud, and as he wept he dug into the earth with a bamboo skewer. When he had dug more than two inches deep he suddenly discovered a bright white relic, clear and translucent, as large as a soybean. Overjoyed, Master Yiru treasured it as a precious jewel.
At that time many saw the Elder sitting cross-legged amid the relics; in one of the relics even his long eyebrows could be seen clearly. That relic is still kept in the relic pagoda.
At that time some who wished to slander the Elder said that his relics had been produced by burning amber mixed in. So some tried putting amber into the fire, and it all turned to ash.

When the Elder departed, the situation was tense, and on the mountain a campaign of ideological rectification was under way, so nothing could be made public. Hence, of the relics he left behind, there were many conflicting accounts and no accurate count could be made. Some said there were only a hundred-odd, but the actual number far exceeded that, the smallest ones being countless and beyond all reckoning; some said there were over a thousand, but there was no way to verify them any longer.

The Elder's deeds in life were many indeed, and are recorded in his chronological biography. The older people at the time all said they had seen and heard these things with their own eyes and ears, and that they are true and not false.

Because of my limited attainments and the short time I spent near the Elder, I can only touch upon a little of his story. I hope that all the great worthies will be compassionate and correct my faults. I shall stop here today. Thank you all.
Homage to the Elder Master Xuyun!
